records.table: Johnnie Walker Black Label 12 Year Old is the Kilmarnock house's aged blend, every whisky in it at least twelve years old. Cardhu's fruit, Glenkinchie's toffee and a soft wisp of Caol Ila smoke make it a neat pour or a rich highball.
records.story: John Walker (1805 to 1857) opened a grocery in Kilmarnock in 1820, after his father's death, and sold whisky among his groceries. His son Alexander Walker (1837 to 1889) took over the business on John's death in 1857 and made it a whisky house: in the 1860s he sold a blend of his own, Old Highland Whisky, and the house's archive dates its slanted label to that decade. In 1893 the firm bought Cardhu on Speyside, its first distillery, and Cardhu malt has stood in the blends ever since. Alexander's sons widened the range and sold it by the colour of its labels, and in 1908 the Striding Man was drawn for the brand. In 1909 the aged blend, Extra Special Old Highland Whisky, was renamed Black Label, since buyers were already asking for it by its label; it has carried twelve years from the start. Behind a bar it is the aged blend to know first: twelve years, malts from across Scotland and a little smoke, and the label a guest names when asking for Scotch by colour.

records.table: Chivas Regal 12 Year Old is the Aberdeen house's honeyed Speyside blend, built around Strathisla malt from Keith with Strathclyde grain. Expect orchard fruit, honey, vanilla and hazelnut; pour it neat, over ice or long with soda.
records.story: The firm traces itself to a grocery opened on King Street in Aberdeen in 1801, which the Chivas brothers came to run, and in 1843, by the house's account, Queen Victoria granted it a Royal Warrant as grocers to the royal household. Chivas Brothers blended whisky in its own cellars for Aberdeen customers who asked for a softer dram, and in 1909 it launched Chivas Regal, an aged blend that the house says first carried twenty-five years. American Prohibition from 1920 cut off much of that trade, and in 1938, by the house's account, it came back with Chivas Regal 12 Year Old. In 1949 the Seagram company bought Chivas Brothers, and in 1950 it bought the Strathisla distillery at Keith, whose malt became the heart of every Chivas blend. In 2001 Pernod Ricard bought Chivas Brothers as Seagram's drinks business was divided. For a bartender the twelve year old is the honeyed Speyside answer to the smokier Johnnie Walker Black Label, and the second aged blend to know by heart.

records.table: Dewar's White Label is the Perth house's blended Scotch, built around honeyed Aberfeldy malt since 1899. Light, with heather honey, pear and vanilla fudge, it belongs in a highball: long with soda or ginger ale, over plenty of ice.
records.story: John Dewar (1805 to 1880) left a family partnership to open his own wine and spirits shop on the High Street of Perth in 1846, and he sold whisky in glass bottles under his own name. On his death in 1880 the firm passed to his sons: the elder ran it in Scotland, and the younger became its salesman in London and abroad. In 1893 Queen Victoria granted John Dewar & Sons a Royal Warrant. The brothers built a distillery of their own at Aberfeldy in Perthshire, which began distilling in 1898, to make the malt at the heart of the house's blends. In 1899 the firm's first master blender from outside the family created White Label, with Aberfeldy at its core. In 1925 John Dewar & Sons joined the Distillers Company, and in 1998 Bacardi bought Dewar's together with four malt distilleries, Aberfeldy among them. The house tells of double ageing: once the whiskies are blended, they rest again in oak before bottling. Behind a bar White Label is the blend for a Scotch and soda, light enough to stretch and honeyed enough to hold its own.

records.story: Matthew Gloag & Son began as a family grocery and wine business on Atholl Street in Perth, and the Gloags ran it for generations. In the late 1890s the founder's grandson launched a blend he called The Grouse Brand, after the game bird of the Scottish moors, and his daughter drew the bird for the label. In 1905, when the business became a limited company, the blend took the name The Famous Grouse; by most accounts the name grew with its popularity. The family kept the firm until 1970, when the sudden death of its chairman left heavy death duties, and the business was sold to Highland Distillers that same year. Glenturret, near Crieff, later housed The Famous Grouse Experience, and a peated Glenturret malt goes into the smoky version of the blend. The house leans on former sherry casks, which give the core blend its oak and toffee. Behind a bar it is the everyday Perth blend to know: soft, sherried and even, a house pour long with soda and a sound base for a Whisky Mac.

records.table: Ballantine's Finest is the Edinburgh house's light, sweet blend, made since 1910, with honey, milk chocolate, red apple and vanilla. It is a Scotch for mixing: over ice, long with soda, or stirred into a Rob Roy.
records.story: Ballantine's began in 1827, when a young grocer whose surname the label carries opened a shop in the Cowgate of Edinburgh. He moved into wines and spirits, and in the 1860s the business went west to Glasgow, where it grew into a blending house. In 1895 Queen Victoria granted the firm a Royal Warrant, and in 1910 it launched Ballantine's Finest, the blend it has kept as its standard ever since. In 1938 Hiram Walker, the Canadian distiller that had bought the firm after American Prohibition ended, completed a grain distillery at Dumbarton on the Clyde. The same year the Lord Lyon granted Ballantine's a coat of arms. From 1959, by the house's telling, a flock of white geese known as the Scotch Watch guarded the Dumbarton warehouses against intruders in place of dogs. For a bartender Ballantine's Finest is the light, everyday blend to set beside the heavier, older names: soft and sweet, easy to stretch with soda, and the Scotch to reach for when a drink wants whisky without smoke.
